title: The Festival for Usha
subtitle: The Vana campaign closes as the Yadu household welcomes a new daughter-in-law
story:
They had ridden out to war and were coming home with a bride.

Dwaraka had waited out the campaign in anxiety, and its relief poured out when the army returned: Aniruddha safe, the war over, and the girl he had been carried off for riding home beside him. Ahuka, the elder of the Yadu house, met Krishna with eyes wide with joy. Seeing him safely returned, he said, the whole family was rejoicing; now let a great festival be undertaken for Aniruddha's return and wedding. Usha, encircled by her friends, was living in the greatest happiness, and the maidens of the palace were already celebrating on their own — some playing on musical instruments, some dancing, some singing, some conversing with one another, some absorbed in chess, some, under the influence of wine, wandering from one group to another. Ahuka added a practical note: the daughter of Kumbhanda should be enlisted as Usha's companion and given to Shamba, and the remaining maidens duly given to the other princes. A festival should take place both in Krishna's residence and in Aniruddha's. And he ended with words that settled the matter: "Usha is encircled by her companions; take her into the palace. The noble daughter of Bana is a worthy daughter-in-law of our race. Welcome her with all dignity."

So it was done. The women of the household, performing benedictory ceremonies as laid down in the ritual code, conducted Usha to Aniruddha's house. When Devaki saw Aniruddha again she shed tears of joy, and so did Revati and Rukmini, the princess of Vidarbha. The damsels blew on bugles and performed benedictions as the bride was taken into the room, and Usha, under the shelter of the Yadu chiefs, lived in their palace and enjoyed the best of happiness.

The household had one more secret to let go. After a few days, Chitralekha — the Apsara who had lived among them in the guise of a mortal woman, the one who had brought Usha and Aniruddha together — took leave with the permission of Usha and her companions and departed for the celestial region. The magic that had begun the romance withdrew, and what remained was ordinary family life.

The first of the Yadu ladies to make Usha her own was Mayavati, Pradyumna's wife, who invited the young Asura princess to her residence and welcomed her youthful daughter-in-law with costly jewels and dresses. Then, according to the custom of the family, all the ladies of the Yadu race duly treated the new daughter-in-law.

And so the long campaign that had begun with a prince stolen in the night ended with a household learning a new daughter-in-law's name. The Vana episode was closed: the enemy spared, the merciful minister rewarded, the city at peace. In the palace of Dwaraka, a girl from the demon city of Sonitpura was learning, day by day, to be at home. And Krishna, encircled by the Yadavas and enjoying the highest prosperity, lived on in Dwaraka and governed the whole world — the war for Aniruddha remembered, in the end, as the war that ended in a wedding.
reflection: The war ends inside the household: the decisive ceremonies are performed by women, and the tears of joy belong to the mothers. An enemy king's daughter becomes the family's own not by decree alone but by being conducted, blessed, gifted and embraced.
next_story_tease: But the house of Yadu had been built on an older night's exchange, when a prison in Mathura gave up one child and took another.
